essays.stem: Describe the consultation and the nail and skin analysis you would carry out before a manicure or pedicure.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the client, seat her comfortably and explain the service. I ask about her health, including diabetes, circulation problems, recent injuries and allergies to nail products or latex. I ask about her job, hobbies and home care, because these affect her nails and the shape and colour she can wear. I ask what she wants from the service. Then I wash my hands and look closely at her hands or feet and nails in good light. I check the skin for dryness, hard skin, cuts, redness, swelling and signs of infection such as athlete's foot or warts. I check the nails for shape, length, strength, ridges, white spots, splitting, lifting, bruising or fungal infection. If I find a contraindication, I explain it kindly and refer her. If not, I suggest the treatment, the shape and the products, and agree the price in J$. I write everything on the record card and the client signs it.
markingPoints: Asks about health, allergies, job and lifestyle
Asks what she wants from the service
Checks the skin for dryness, hard skin, cuts and infection
Checks the nails for shape, strength and conditions
Acts on contraindications, agrees the plan and price, and records it with her signature

essays.stem: Explain which conditions would stop or restrict a manicure or pedicure, and how you would deal with a client who has diabetes.
essays.modelAnswer: Infections stop the service, because they can spread to the therapist, the tools and other clients. These include fungal infections such as athlete's foot or a fungal nail, bacterial infections such as paronychia, with red, swollen, painful skin, and viral infections such as warts and verrucae. Severe nail lifting, broken or bleeding skin, swelling, a recent fracture or sprain, and inflamed skin also stop the service on that area. I explain kindly and refer the client to a doctor or pharmacist, and to a podiatrist for ingrown toenails or corns. Some conditions restrict the service: a small cut or bruise is avoided, and varicose veins are not massaged. A client with diabetes may have poor circulation and less feeling in her feet, and small cuts can heal slowly and become infected. I ask for her doctor's advice, use warm, not hot, water, file instead of cutting where possible, do not cut the cuticles, take great care with hard skin and check her feet carefully. I record it all.
markingPoints: Names infections that stop the service (fungal, bacterial, viral) and says why
Names other conditions that stop it (broken skin, swelling, fracture, severe lifting)
Refers correctly (doctor, pharmacist, podiatrist) and explains kindly
Names conditions that restrict it (cuts, bruises, varicose veins)
Diabetes: explains the risks and the extra care, with a doctor's advice

essays.stem: Describe how you would keep a manicure and pedicure service hygienic, including the care of tools and the foot spa.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash my hands before and after each client, and the client's hands or feet are cleaned before the service. I use fresh towels for every client. Metal tools, such as nippers, clippers and pushers, are cleaned with soap and water and a brush to remove skin and dust, then fully immersed in a salon disinfectant for the time the maker gives, or sterilised in an autoclave. Clean tools are stored in a clean, covered container, and a UV cabinet is used only for storing clean tools. Single-use items, such as emery boards, buffers, orange sticks, pumice, toe separators and cotton, are used once and thrown away. Any blade goes in the sharps box. After every client, the foot spa is drained, scrubbed to remove debris, rinsed and then disinfected as the maker says, including the jets of a whirlpool spa, and the cleaning is written in the log. I wear gloves where there is a risk of blood, and if a cut happens I press with clean cotton, apply antiseptic and dispose of the cotton in a sealed bag.
markingPoints: Hand washing and fresh towels for every client
Metal tools cleaned, then disinfected or sterilised, and stored correctly
Single-use items used once; sharps in a sharps box
Foot spa cleaned and disinfected after every client, as the maker says, and logged
Gloves where needed and correct action for a cut

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would carry out a full manicure with a hand massage and polish.
essays.modelAnswer: After the consultation, I wash my hands and clean the client's hands. I remove old polish, pressing a soaked cotton pad on each nail and wiping from base to tip. I file each nail to the agreed shape with a fine file, from the side to the centre in one direction. I apply cuticle remover or softener and soak the fingers in a finger bowl of warm soapy water. I dry the hands and push the cuticles back gently with a pusher or a wrapped orange stick, and trim only hangnails and loose dead skin with nippers. I clean under the free edge and buff the nails if needed. I give a hand and arm massage with cream, using effleurage, petrissage and friction movements. Then I remove all oil from the nail plates with remover. I apply a thin base coat, two thin coats of colour and a top coat, capping the free edge each time. I check the finish, give aftercare advice and record the service.
markingPoints: Removes old polish and shapes the nails correctly
Softens, soaks and pushes back the cuticles gently; nips only dead skin
Gives a hand and arm massage with suitable movements
Removes oil from the nail plates before polishing
Base coat, two thin colour coats and top coat, capped; aftercare and record

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would carry out a full pedicure with a foot massage and polish.
essays.modelAnswer: After the consultation and a careful check of the feet, I seat the client comfortably with her feet raised. I wash my hands and put on gloves if needed. I remove old polish and soak her feet in a clean, disinfected foot spa or basin of warm water for a few minutes. I dry one foot and cut the toenails straight across with toenail clippers, then smooth the edges with a file. I apply cuticle remover, push the cuticles back gently and remove only loose dead skin. I smooth hard skin on the heels and balls of the feet gently with a foot file or pumice, leaving some for protection, and use a foot scrub. I rinse and dry the feet well, especially between the toes. I give a foot and lower leg massage with cream, avoiding any varicose veins. I remove the oil from the nail plates, place toe separators, and apply base coat, two thin coats of colour and top coat. The client wears open-toed slippers while it dries. I give aftercare and record the service.
markingPoints: Checks the feet, positions the client and soaks in a clean, disinfected basin
Cuts toenails straight across and smooths the edges
Gentle cuticle work and safe hard-skin removal, leaving some for protection
Dries between the toes and gives a foot and leg massage, avoiding varicose veins
Removes oil, uses toe separators, polishes correctly; aftercare and record

essays.stem: Describe the massage movements you would use in a hand and arm massage, the effects of each, and when you would change or leave out the massage.
essays.modelAnswer: I apply a hand cream or massage lotion and begin with effleurage. This is a smooth, gliding stroke from the fingers up the arm towards the elbow. It spreads the cream, warms the skin and relaxes the client, and I also use it between other movements and to finish. Petrissage is kneading: I lift and squeeze the muscles of the forearm and the palm gently. It improves blood flow and eases tight muscles. Frictions are small, firm circles with the thumbs, around the joints and across the back of the hand, to loosen stiffness. I can also gently move each finger joint through its normal range. I keep an even rhythm and pressure, and keep one hand in contact with the client all the time. I leave out or change the massage over cuts, bruises, swelling, skin infections, recent injuries, or very painful joints. For a client with arthritis I use very light pressure, or leave it out if her doctor advises.
markingPoints: Effleurage: describes it and its effects
Petrissage: describes it and its effects
Frictions or joint movements: describes them and their effects
Even rhythm and pressure, keeping contact with the client
Says when to change or leave out the massage

essays.stem: Describe the main parts of the nail and explain why a therapist must know them to work safely.
essays.modelAnswer: The nail plate is the hard, see-through part that we file and paint. It sits on the nail bed, the skin underneath, which holds it in place and gives it a pink colour. The free edge is the part of the plate that grows past the end of the finger or toe, and under it is the hyponychium, a seal of skin that keeps germs out. The matrix lies under the skin at the base of the nail. It is the living part that makes new nail cells, and the lunula, the pale half-moon, is the part of it we can see. The cuticle is the dead skin that sticks to the nail plate, and the eponychium is the living fold of skin at the base. The nail walls and grooves run along the sides. I must know these parts because pressing hard on the matrix can damage the new nail, cutting the living eponychium or hyponychium can let in infection, and digging into the side grooves can cause ingrown nails.
markingPoints: Nail plate, nail bed and free edge described correctly
Matrix described as the growing part, with the lunula
Cuticle and eponychium described and told apart
Hyponychium and nail walls or grooves described
Explains why the knowledge keeps the client safe (matrix, living skin, infection)

essays.stem: Describe how you would apply nail polish so that it looks neat and lasts, including a French manicure finish.
essays.modelAnswer: First I remove all oil from the nail plates with remover, because oil stops the polish from sticking. I apply a thin base coat to protect the nail and help the colour stick, and cap the free edge. For the colour, I roll the bottle between my palms to mix it, rather than shaking it, so that no bubbles form. I wipe one side of the brush on the bottle neck and place it near the base of the nail, leaving a tiny gap at the cuticle. I use about three strokes: one down the centre and one down each side, keeping the coat thin and even. I apply a second thin coat after the first has dried a little, and cap the free edge each time. I clean any polish off the skin with a fine brush dipped in remover. Then I apply a top coat and cap it. For a French finish, I paint a curved white smile line on the tip, then a sheer pink or nude colour, and seal with top coat.
markingPoints: Removes oil from the nail plates first
Base coat applied and capped
Mixes polish by rolling; about three strokes in thin coats with a small gap at the cuticle
Caps each coat, cleans the skin and finishes with top coat
Describes a French finish correctly (white smile line, sheer colour, top coat)

essays.stem: Explain the health and safety points you would follow during a pedicure, including electrical safety, chemicals and slips.
essays.modelAnswer: Water and electricity are a dangerous mix. Before using an electric foot spa, I check the plug and cable for damage, keep the socket and cable away from water, and fill or empty the spa only as the maker says. I never use faulty equipment; I label it and report it. Water on the floor can cause slips, so I put towels down, wipe up splashes at once and help the client in and out of the chair. Nail products such as polish remover and polish give off fumes and can catch fire, so I keep the room ventilated, keep lids closed and keep products away from heat and flames. I wear gloves when using disinfectant and follow the maker's instructions for dilution and contact time. I keep the safety data sheets to hand. I sit with a straight back and raise the client's foot on a rest to protect my back. If I cut the skin, I wear gloves, press with clean cotton, apply antiseptic and record it.
markingPoints: Electrical safety with the foot spa: checks, keeps water away, reports faults
Prevents slips by controlling water on the floor and helping the client
Ventilation, fire safety and storage of nail products
Gloves and correct use of disinfectant; safety data sheets
Good posture and correct first aid for a cut

essays.stem: Describe the aftercare and home-care advice you would give after a manicure and a pedicure, and how you would recommend products and rebooking.
essays.modelAnswer: After a manicure, the client should wear gloves for housework, washing and gardening, and should not use her nails as tools. She should apply hand cream several times a day and cuticle oil each night, and file any rough edge with a fine file in one direction. She should add a thin top coat every few days to make the polish last, and use a sunscreen on her hands. After a pedicure, she should wash and dry her feet well every day, especially between the toes, wear clean socks and well-fitting shoes, and use a foot cream on the heels, but not between the toes. She should cut her toenails straight across and see a podiatrist for corns or ingrown nails. I may suggest a product I used, such as cuticle oil or foot cream, if it meets her needs, and give the price in J$ without pressure. I suggest she rebooks in about two to four weeks and write the advice on her record card.
markingPoints: Manicure aftercare: gloves, no nails as tools, hand cream and cuticle oil
Polish care: top coat, filing in one direction
Pedicure aftercare: dry between toes, good shoes, foot cream, cut nails straight
Recommends products honestly with the price
Rebooks and records the advice

practical1.title: Full manicure with a hand and arm massage and polish
practical1.brief: Work in pairs in the Centre's salon and take turns as therapist and client. In a group of five, one member works on a model who has agreed to take part. Each member sets up a hygienic manicure station, holds a consultation, checks the client's hands and nails for contraindications and completes the record card. She then gives a full manicure: removing old polish, shaping, cuticle care, a hand and arm massage, cleaning the nail plates, and a base coat, two coats of colour and a top coat (or a buffed finish for a client who does not want polish). She gives aftercare advice. Each member also takes one job for the group: setting up and disinfecting the stations, preparing the finger bowls, taking the photos, or cleaning and disinfecting the tools at the end. Photograph each stage below. Photos show the hands and nails only. Hand in once for the whole group, with the record cards.

Cuticle remover, cuticle oil and hand cream

practical2.title: Full pedicure with a foot and lower leg massage and polish
practical2.brief: Work in pairs in the Centre's salon and take turns as therapist and client; in a group of five, one member works on a model who has agreed. Each member checks that the foot spa or basin has been cleaned and disinfected, holds a consultation, checks the client's feet carefully, including between the toes, and completes the record card. Anyone with a contraindication on the feet is not treated, and her partner works on a model instead. Each member then gives a full pedicure: removing old polish, soaking, cutting the toenails straight across and filing them, cuticle care, gentle hard-skin removal with a foot file, a foot scrub, a foot and lower leg massage, cleaning the nail plates, and polish with toe separators. She gives aftercare advice. At the end, each member cleans and disinfects her foot spa or basin as the maker says and fills in the cleaning log. Each member also takes one job for the group: setting up, keeping the floor dry and safe, taking the photos, or checking the cleaning log. Photograph each stage below. Photos show the feet and the work area only. Hand in once for the whole group.

Toenail clippers and cuticle nippers (cleaned and disinfected), cuticle pushers and orange sticks
Foot files, single-use files and toe separators
Nail polish remover, cotton, base coat, polishes and top coat
Record cards and the foot spa cleaning log
Salon disinfectant, gloves, a lined, lidded bin and the sharps box
